fatal_errors: The proposed lattice-distortion mechanism does not reconstruct the governing Cr2O3-scale mechanism or the effect of Cr-depleted L12/L21 precipitates and matrix–precipitate interfaces.
The intervention omits the actual comparison between the as-printed single-fcc alloy and the alloy aged at 750°C for 50 h.
The predicted improvement conflicts with the observed result that the precipitation-aged state gained more mass, especially at higher temperatures.
The baseline is not operationally defined: changing composition or microstructure to remove lattice distortion also changes oxidation-active chemistry and diffusion pathways.
No supporting evidence or direct measurement of lattice distortion, oxygen diffusivity, or scale transport is supplied.
explanation: The hypothesis addresses high-temperature oxidation in multiprincipal-element alloys, and its nominal 800–1200°C range overlaps part of the target range. Otherwise, it is largely disconnected from the study. The target behavior is governed by formation of a continuous Cr-rich, primarily Cr2O3 barrier; aging creates Cr-depleted precipitates and additional interfaces that delay this protection and may provide short-circuit oxygen paths. The generated mechanism instead invokes generic lattice-distortion-induced suppression of inward oxygen diffusion and does not account for outward Cr transport, duplex/trilayer scale development, or the temperature-dependent transition in oxidation kinetics. Its proposed comparison varies alloy compositions and microstructures simultaneously, so any oxidation difference could arise from Cr, Al, or Ti activity rather than lattice distortion. A discriminating test would require composition-matched states, quantified precipitate and Cr distributions, time-resolved mass-gain kinetics, cross-sectional scale thickness and chemistry, and ideally direct diffusion measurements. The asserted oxygen pressure and integrity improvement are unsupported by the supplied evidence.
